> We believe that, when the staging primary database becomes unavailable during representative checkout traffic, an eligible replica will become the sole writable primary within 30 seconds. The application will reconnect automatically, checkout latency and error rate will remain within the bounds below, and every acknowledged order will remain durable. Retries and ambiguous timeouts will produce no duplicate orders or charges.

Hold the offered traffic mix constant, including reads and checkout writes, and capture a ten-minute baseline immediately before injection.

| Measure | Proposed admission condition | Hypothesized response |
|---|---|---|
| Checkout request errors | Below 0.1% | Below 2% over the 60-second fault window |
| Checkout p95 latency | Below 300 ms | Below 1 second during the fault window |
| Successful order throughput | At least 50/minute at the fixed offered load | Returns to baseline within 60 seconds of fault onset |
| Database writer | One healthy primary; replica eligible | New sole writer available within 30 seconds |
| Data/payment integrity | Reconciliation clean | Zero lost acknowledged orders, duplicate charges, or corrupted totals |

Also require sustained baseline behavior for five minutes after recovery. Measure failed and timed-out requests separately so disappearing traffic cannot make latency or error metrics look healthy.

Inject primary loss for at most 60 seconds using the database platform's supported, staging-tested mechanism. The blast radius includes the isolated cluster and every staging service dependent on it. Do not assume that an application-side network block necessarily triggers replica promotion.

Before execution, name the experiment owner and backup abort operator. Verify automated stop conditions and rollback in staging.

Abort on detected data corruption/duplicate charging, loss of monitoring, an unrelated incident, or checkout errors above 5% for two consecutive ten-second windows. Configure a self-expiring fault.

on:
  push:

permissions:

concurrency:
  group: tests-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.ref }}

env:

jobs:
  fast:

    timeout-minutes: 10

**Mission:** Explore the new checkout from payment selection through order confirmation, with the available payment methods, provider sandbox fixtures, varied carts, and interrupted sessions, to discover inconsistent payment state, unclear recovery behavior, and requirement gaps when customers change methods or encounter failures.

**Status:** Planned; no exploration has been executed.

**Timebox:** 90 minutes: 15 minutes to orient, 40 minutes to explore method variations, 20 minutes for failures and boundaries, and 15 minutes to document and debrief.

| Area | Questions to pursue |

| Changing methods | What happens when switching methods after entering details, after a decline, or after cancelling a challenge? Does the UI retain valid cart information and discard obsolete payment state? |
| Amounts and eligibility | Do totals, currency, discounts, taxes, and delivery charges stay consistent across method changes? What happens at documented method-specific minimums or maximums? |
| Failures and recovery | Can the customer recover from a decline, expired instrument, challenge failure, or session expiry? Are errors understandable and associated with the relevant input or method? |

Start with **code coverage, flakiness, and defect escape rate** for two sprints. At 20 features per sprint, the immediate question is whether new behavior has meaningful checks and whether those checks catch regressions. Test count alone cannot answer that.

| Metric | Definition and source | Proposed owner | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Code coverage | Executed lines or branches divided by eligible lines or branches; collect the test runner's JSON/LCOV output and show changes by module | A developer responsible for the test framework | Investigate drops in critical modules and add assertions for the missing behavior |
| Flakiness | Test executions with inconsistent results on unchanged code and equivalent inputs, divided by eligible test executions; retain attempt-level CI results | A QA/test-infrastructure owner | Triage the top recurring cases, with an owner and expiry for any quarantine |
| Defect escape rate | Production defects divided by all defects found for the same release cohort and observation period | Engineering lead | Classify each serious escape and add the lowest-cost regression that would have caught it |

**First two weeks:** establish the baseline. Save commit, test identity, attempt, outcome, duration and environment with CI results. Keep failed, skipped and unrun tests distinct. A green retry is evidence of inconsistency, not proof of a root cause. Label production issues consistently, deduplicate reports of the same defect, and use the same observation window when comparing releases. If a denominator is zero or unknown, display “not available,” not zero percent.

**Weeks three and four:** add a small trend view with the current value, baseline, target, owner and links to the underlying failures. Spend five minutes each week deciding one action from the data. Avoid ranking engineers by these metrics.

Set targets after seeing the baseline and the cost of failures. Reasonable provisional rules are: investigate every critical-path coverage drop, block on a failed required critical test, and investigate repeated flaky failures promptly. Percentage goals should be team decisions, not copied release approvals.

For the 20 shipped features, attach acceptance criteria to their tests or documented exploratory checks. Review gaps in high-risk features; do not require an arbitrary number of tests per feature. Add CI duration or recovery time later when a concrete decision needs them.

Before enforcing any new gate, show that it rejects a deliberately broken fixture and passes its known-good counterpart. This is a rollout plan; no baseline or dashboard data has been collected yet. Which CI system and bug tracker hold your existing results?

Start with **qa-start’s three-step sequence: project context → test strategy → first test plan**. This gives the team a shared answer to what matters, how to verify it, and what to do first.

### 1. Capture the project context

Use **qa-project-context** to prepare `.agents/qa-project-context.md`. Record:

- Product purpose, users, and the first release’s critical journeys.
- Stack, repository structure, deployment process, and available environments.
- External dependencies, sensitive data, and consequences of failure.
- Team ownership, available QA capacity, and current tooling.
- Initial quality goals and the areas with the greatest uncertainty.

Discover what the repository can answer and ask the team about business risks and commitments. Unknowns should remain explicit; a proposed tool or target is not an existing capability.

**Completion criterion:** the context document is filled in sufficiently to guide decisions without repeatedly asking the same setup questions.

### 2. Agree on a short test strategy

Run **test-strategy** using that context. Decide:

- Which checks belong at unit, integration, and end-to-end levels.
- Which frameworks fit the actual stack and the team’s skills.
- How test data and environments will remain reproducible.
- What must pass on a pull request and before release.
- Who owns failures, exploratory testing, and maintaining the suite.

Start with fast tests for business logic and service boundaries, plus a small set of critical user journeys. Choose the balance from the product’s risks; there is no universal test-pyramid percentage.

**Completion criterion:** a concise strategy, such as `strategy.md`, explains the choices, entry/exit criteria, and quality gates.

### 3. Create the first executable test plan

Run **test-planning** for the first sprint or release. For each in-scope feature, record its scenarios, risk/priority, test level, owner, estimated effort, required data, and any deferred coverage.

**Completion criterion:** `plan.md` tells someone exactly what to test next and what is outside the current scope.

Then implement the highest-priority checks, add the appropriate automation framework, and run the suite in CI on pull requests. Once it runs consistently, establish a small set of quality metrics.

To tailor the first step, what are you building, which stack are you using, and which customer journey must work for the first release?

**Initial classification: a business-logic error involving a currency edge case. The primary test level that should have caught it is unit testing.** That conclusion assumes the discount calculation or eligibility logic behaves incorrectly when passed a supported non-USD currency.

| Dimension | Classification |
|---|---|
| Root-cause category | Logic error: incomplete or incorrect currency-dependent discount behavior |
| Should-catch level | Unit: calculation, eligibility, currency representation, and rounding boundaries |
| Prevention opportunity | Add the missing regression scenario, or expand an existing USD-only parameterized test |

This is a provisional technical classification, not a completed root-cause analysis. If the calculation works correctly in isolation but an API drops or rewrites the currency, classify the defect as an **integration failure**, primarily caught by integration tests. If support for the currency was never specified, a requirements gap may be a contributing cause.

### Establish the evidence

Obtain the affected currency, discount rule, input subtotal, expected total, actual total, and the introducing change. Reconstruct introduced → released → detected → resolved from commits, deployment records, and the defect ticket. Impact, severity, existing coverage, and detection/fix times are currently unknown.

Review the relevant tests before concluding that they were absent. A test may have used only USD, asserted only that a request succeeded, or reproduced the implementation’s incorrect assumption.

### Add a regression at the smallest useful boundary

For example, **if the agreed rule is a currency-independent 10% discount**, a EUR subtotal of 10,000 minor units should produce a 1,000-unit discount and a 9,000-unit total. The unit test should fail against the faulty implementation and pass after the correction. Also cover the affected currency’s actual rounding and eligibility boundaries; do not assume every currency uses two decimal places.

Add an integration case verifying that checkout passes the currency and persists the discounted total correctly. A representative non-USD checkout E2E test adds journey coverage, but the calculation defect should be detected earlier.

|---|---|---|---|
| Fix the defect and add its unit regression | Calculation maintainer | Before the fix is released | Fails on faulty code; passes with fix in CI |

| Add supported-currency examples to refinement and fixtures | QA/product representative | Next sprint | Updated criteria and fixtures reviewed |

Use an evidence-backed release record for the **exact payment release candidate**. This is a proposed checklist; readiness cannot be established without the results.

Record the version/build SHA, configuration and migration versions, release scope, named approver, on-call engineer, evidence links, and decision timestamp.

### Mandatory go/no-go checks

| Check | Evidence required |
|---|---|
| CI passes | Unit, integration, critical E2E, contract, type, and lint results for this candidate |
| Payment correctness | Exact amount/currency/discount/tax assertions across supported cases; authorization, capture, decline, cancellation, and refund paths where changed |
| Transaction integrity | Duplicate submit and retry tests; idempotency; payment-success/order-write-failure recovery; webhook signature, duplicate, and ordering tests |
| No release blockers | No unresolved P0/P1 defects; each accepted lower-severity issue has impact, mitigation, and an owner |
| Performance | Checkout and provider-facing latency/error results within agreed budgets under representative concurrency |
| Security | No unresolved high/critical findings; ownership checks and secret/logging protections verified for changed paths |
| Production configuration | Provider endpoints, credentials, webhook destinations, feature flags, and compatibility checked against the intended production configuration |
| Data changes | Forward migration tested; previous application version remains compatible, or a documented forward-recovery plan exists |
| Operations | Payment success, duplicate-charge, reconciliation, latency, and error signals visible; alerts tested; on-call available |
| Recovery | Previous artifact available; kill switch/code rollback practiced and timed in staging; recovery owner and commands documented |
| Release coordination | Release notes, support briefing draft, deployment window, dependency changes, and conflicting releases reviewed |

Every mandatory item needs a passing result or a demonstrably inapplicable scope note. Unmeasured payment integrity or an untested recovery path means **NO-GO**.

### Smoke tests

Keep staging smoke coverage under five minutes: application health, authentication, checkout submission with provider sandbox credentials, matching order confirmation, and order retrieval. The detailed error and concurrency cases belong in regression tests.

Run production smoke checks within 60 seconds of deployment: application health, login, protected reads, and API responses using dedicated synthetic accounts. Exercise payment completion only through a verified isolated sandbox path; otherwise omit the charge from production smoke checks.

### Staged rollout and stop rules

Proposed stages: **1% for 15–30 minutes → 10% for one hour → 50% for two hours → 100%, monitored for 24 hours**.

Capture a comparable pre-release baseline and compare candidate/control cohorts by provider and currency. Promote only with sufficient samples, no new exception classes, stable payment success/reconciliation, and latency/error rates within agreed tolerances. A starting tolerance is 1.2× baseline for P95 and 5xx; tune it before release. Low traffic extends observation.

Pre-agree rollback triggers: 5xx above 2× baseline for five minutes, P95 above 3× for five minutes, or three consecutive health-check failures. Define an absolute floor and sample requirement when the baseline is near zero. Confirmed duplicate charges, unauthorized access, or ledger corruption trigger immediate containment.

Disable the affected feature or restore the previous compatible artifact, then rerun smoke checks and verify recovery. A code rollback does not reverse settled payments; reconcile and repair financial records separately.

**GO requires completed evidence and named, timestamped sign-off.** Continue checks at 0–15 minutes, two hours, and 24 hours, including delayed webhooks and reconciliation jobs.

**Score = impact × probability.** Impact ranges from 1 (negligible) to 5 (catastrophic); probability ranges from 1 (rare) to 5 (frequent).

| Failure mode | Impact | Probability | Score | Zone |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Payment succeeds but no order is recorded | 5 | 4 | 20 | CRITICAL |
| Retry or double submit creates duplicate charges | 5 | 3 | 15 | CRITICAL |
| Discounts, currency rounding, or tax rules produce incorrect totals | 4 | 4 | 16 | CRITICAL |
| Provider timeout/outage prevents checkout completion | 5 | 3 | 15 | CRITICAL |
| Concurrent purchases oversell the last item | 4 | 3 | 12 | HIGH |
| A customer can access another customer’s order | 5 | 2 | 10 | HIGH |
| Valid international address is rejected, requiring a workaround | 3 | 3 | 9 | MEDIUM |

| Summary alignment is wrong but checkout remains usable | 2 | 2 | 4 | LOW |
| Internal diagnostic label has a typo | 1 | 1 | 1 | LOW |

The zone boundaries are **CRITICAL 15–25; HIGH 10–14; MEDIUM 5–9; LOW 1–4**. Thus a score of 15 belongs in CRITICAL.

Current mitigations are **unverified for every row**. The final column identifies the evidence or protection to establish, not a claim that your system lacks it.

| Risk | Trigger | Blast radius | Detection | Mitigation/evidence gap to resolve |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Charged without order | Callback races with a failed database write | Affected purchasers and fulfillment | Payment/order reconciliation | Fault-injection test; durable recovery/reconciliation evidence |
| Duplicate charge | Replay, retry, or repeated submit | Affected purchasers and support | Duplicate transaction alert | Prove one financial effect per idempotency key |
| Incorrect total | Stacked discounts, boundary amounts, currency/tax branches | Customers using affected rules | Expected-vs-charged comparison | Parameterized calculation tests and persisted-total checks |

| Zone | Proposed coverage |
|---|---|
| CRITICAL | Full business-rule automation, all service boundaries, journey/error-path E2E, concurrency/load tests, release exploration, real-time monitoring; target 90%+ relevant branch coverage |
| HIGH | Full risk-scenario automation, key integrations, happy path/top errors, periodic manual review; target 80%+ relevant branch coverage |
| MEDIUM | Happy path and key errors; target 70%+ relevant branch coverage |
| LOW | Proportionate manual checks; basic unit coverage where useful |

These percentage targets are planning aids, not proof of correctness. Compare them with actual coverage and assign each gap a priority, named owner, and target sprint; these remain unassigned here.

**Timing or environment differences are the leading hypotheses, but “passes locally” alone does not identify the cause.** Apply the decision tree using repeated runs of the same commit and equivalent configuration.

### 1. Does it consistently pass alone in CI?

Run only the affected test repeatedly, then compare it with the full suite under the normal CI worker count.

- **Another test creates state this test requires:** suspect **order dependency**. Give this test its own setup; confirm it works without its predecessor.
- **Tests share a database row, cache key, file, account, or queue:** suspect **data dependency**. Look for conflicting writes and failed cleanup; isolate data per test/worker.
- **It passes with one worker but fails under parallel load without shared state:** investigate **environment contention or timing** as well. Isolation success is evidence, not proof of a data problem.

If this is Playwright, a starting reproduction command is:

```bash
npx playwright test path/to/flaky.spec.ts --repeat-each=20 --workers=1 --retries=0 --trace=on
```

Use a specific test filter if the file contains several tests. Capture normal parallel CI results too, rather than changing every variable at once.

| Evidence | Likely category | Next check |
|---|---|---|
| Locator/assertion timeout | Timing | Did the action precede rendering, hydration, an animation, or a response? |
| Connection refused or connection timeout | Environment | Dependency readiness, DNS, service logs, network route |
| OOM, disk exhaustion, browser crashes | Environment | Memory/CPU/disk and worker count |
| Failure concentrated on one runner/image | Environment | Browser/runtime versions, installed fonts, locale and resources |

import json
import coverage

cov = coverage.Coverage(data_file=".coverage")
cov.load()
data = cov.get_data()
if not data.has_arcs():
    raise RuntimeError("Capture branch coverage first")

files = sorted(data.measured_files())
statements, excluded, branch_sites = {}, {}, {}
context_files = defaultdict(set)

# Analyze source once, before applying context filters.
for filename in files:
    _, executable, ignored, _, _ = cov.analysis2(filename)
    statements[filename] = set(executable) - set(ignored)
    excluded[filename] = set(ignored)
    branch_sites[filename] = set(cov.branch_stats(filename))
    for contexts in data.contexts_by_lineno(filename).values():
        for context in contexts:
            context_files[context].add(filename)

lines, branches = defaultdict(set), defaultdict(set)
for context, touched_files in context_files.items():
    test_id, separator, phase = context.rpartition("|")
    if not separator or phase not in {"setup", "run", "teardown"}:
        continue  # Startup/unattributed coverage is not a test.
    data.set_query_context(context)  # Exact match, safe for parameter IDs.
    for filename in touched_files:
        lines[test_id].update(
            (filename, number)
            for number in data.lines(filename) or []
            if number in statements[filename]
        )
        branches[test_id].update(
            (filename, start, end)
            for start, end in data.arcs(filename) or []
            if start in branch_sites[filename]
            and end not in excluded[filename]
        )

data.set_query_contexts(None)
line_owners = Counter(item for items in lines.values() for item in items)
branch_owners = Counter(item for items in branches.values() for item in items)

rows = []
for test_id in sorted(set(lines) | set(branches)):
    rows.append({
        "test_id": test_id,
        "lines": sorted(lines[test_id]),
        "branches": sorted(branches[test_id]),

        ),
        "unique_branches": sorted(
            item for item in branches[test_id] if branch_owners[item] == 1

| Targeting | ON account receives new flow; OFF account and unrelated users retain legacy flow |
| ON → OFF | Existing carts remain usable; no lost orders or duplicate submissions; new checkouts take the recovery path |

For both variants, cover success, decline, timeout/retry, double-click, interrupted return navigation, authorization boundaries, and duplicate/delayed payment callbacks. Test interactions with other checkout flags using all-legacy, all-new, and risk-relevant mixed combinations.

Decide whether a checkout’s variant is fixed at creation. Test rollback against records created by the new flow; disabling the flag cannot undo an incompatible schema or already-triggered payment.

### Safe production execution

Use dedicated synthetic tenants excluded from customer analytics, billing, fulfillment, and notifications. Full purchase assertions in production require verified routing of those tenants to payment test mode and isolated downstream side effects. Otherwise, limit production probes to rendering/read-only checks and perform transaction completion in the provider sandbox before rollout.

### Rollout and gates

Progress through internal users, **1% → 10% → 50% → 100%**. Initial minimum observation windows: **30 minutes, 2 hours, 4 hours, then 24 hours at full rollout**. Extend them until traffic provides adequate evidence.

Compare ON against a contemporaneous OFF control, segmented by device/payment method. Track payment success, checkout conversion, 5xx/JavaScript errors, latency, duplicate transactions, and reconciliation failures; exclude synthetic probes from business metrics.

Calibrate automated thresholds before launch. Starting proposals: rollback on any confirmed duplicate charge or data-integrity failure; halt/rollback for sustained 5xx above both 2× control and 0.5%, or p95 latency above 1.5× control for five minutes. Define business-metric sample sizes and significance rules from actual traffic; missing data blocks promotion. Include existing SLO/error-budget gates.

### Rollback and retirement

In staging, deliberately trip a guardrail and verify automatic flag disable, legacy smoke success, metric recovery, and on-call notification. Recheck the same evidence after any production rollback; flag rollback need not change the deployed build version.

Assign an owner and expiry. After the agreed stable observation period, review flag removal, retain enabled-path regression tests, and remove obsolete branching through normal code review.
